submitLabel: Your one-page decision, the delta reckoning, and the write-up
intro: Paste the one-page decision with all its terms including what comes off, the delta reckoning across the seven claims you contested in Modules 1–7, your predicted count of true claims scored against the actual, and the 400–500 word write-up. This is the course close. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext: You are grading the closing submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, People Ops & HR Technology track — for People Operations, HR Operations, HRIS and HR Systems professionals who have completed AI 101 and AI 201. Module 8 applied activity, 'Stays on, changes, or comes off'. Three parts. (1) A one-page decision on the capability the learner has tracked since Module 1, with exactly three permitted outcomes — stays on, changes, or comes off — plus the baseline from Module 2 as actual numbers and the query, the 90-day measure and what counts as a move, the funding line naming what they will stop doing, the reinvestment commitment naming where capacity goes specifically enough to be checked in six months, THE SUBTRACTION (what comes off), and the review date with its holder. (2) The delta reckoning: the seven claims contested across Modules 1–7, what they committed at the time and concluded after each, how many turned out true of their organization, which claim moved them most and what specifically moved it, and — the question that matters — which DIRECTION their judgement leans, whether they consistently assumed their organization was in better shape than the evidence showed or worse. (3) A 400–500 word write-up. KEY GRADING INSTRUCTIONS. On the decision: apply the module's own test — is there a state of the world in which they do not proceed? If the vendor is signed, the date announced and the training built, this is a migration, and the graded response is whether the learner NAMED it as one. A learner who writes 'this is a migration, not a bet, and here is why that is the right call' should score at the top of that dimension; a learner who calls a fait accompli a bet should be told which sentence gave it away. Check the funding line is a real activity being stopped rather than a licensing fact. Check the reinvestment commitment names work and whose it is — 'redeployed to higher-value work' is the sentence the module says means nobody has decided. Check the subtraction: 'nothing comes off' is acceptable ONLY with a reason, and the learner was told to check the widest-reach unowned row in their register first. Treat a decision whose outcome is 'comes off' as a strong answer, not a weak one — subtraction reduces the surface every other module governs, and it is the term only this role has. Watch for two failures the exercise teaches: a baseline to be collected after launch, which is Module 2's unrecoverable error; and a funding line that pays for a capability by cancelling the control that would detect it going wrong. On the reckoning: the direction-of-judgement question is the most important thing in the submission. Grade whether the learner actually answered it with a direction and evidence, not whether the direction is flattering. Consistently over-estimating their organization's readiness is the common pattern and naming it honestly is a top-scoring answer. NEVER grade prediction accuracy — grade the account of the gap. The module's claim, which the write-up must take a position on, is that a bet you cannot reverse is a migration and only someone who has performed the rollback can tell the difference. Its real counter-argument is that this valorizes reversibility past usefulness: an HCM implementation, a process redesign retraining thousands, a retired integration and the institutional knowledge that went with it are all irreversible, and organizations that genuinely transformed did so through commitments they could not walk back — irreversibility being the signal the organization meant it. So demanding a rehearsed rollback for everything is a way of never being accountable for a direction, and converts the systems function into a brake. The write-up must say where the line falls between a change requiring reversibility and a commitment that legitimately should not have it, and should notice that the counter-argument is Module 1's own reversibility gate turned against the track's closing artifact. Finally: the write-up must name ONE artifact from the track the learner will keep maintaining and what would have to be true for it to still be current in a year. A commitment to maintain all four is a commitment to maintain none, and should be marked down as such.

opening.label: Predicted — of the 7 claims you contested in Modules 1–7, how many were true of you
opening.hint: From memory, before you go back and read what you wrote. Out of seven.

calibration.label: Actual — how many turned out true, from your own records
calibration.hint: Counted from what you committed and concluded in each module.

dimensions.name: The decision is a decision, and it knows which kind it is
dimensions.criteria: One of three outcomes — stays on, changes, comes off — with all terms present. Then apply the module's test: is there a state of the world in which they do not proceed? A learner whose plan is already committed and who NAMES it a migration rather than a bet scores at the top; a learner who calls a fait accompli a bet should be shown the sentence that gave it away (a signed contract, an announced date, built training, told staff). 'Comes off' as the chosen outcome is a strong answer, not a weak one.

dimensions.name: The baseline and the measure would survive a hostile read
dimensions.criteria: The baseline must be actual numbers with the query, carried from Module 2 — a baseline to be collected after launch is the module's unrecoverable error and must be named as such. The 90-day measure must be one that moves only if things genuinely improved: adoption, satisfaction with the tool, containment and cost per contact all move when a deployment makes things worse for employees, and choosing one of them is the central error the exercise tests. Credit a measure designed to detect the deployment going wrong, and credit a 'comes off' decision that measures whether removal made things worse.

dimensions.name: The funding line, reinvestment and subtraction are real
dimensions.criteria: The funding line must name an activity being stopped and ideally its hours — a licensing fact ('included in our existing subscription') is not a funding line. The reinvestment must name the work and whose it is, specifically enough for someone to check in six months; 'redeployed to higher-value work' is the sentence the module says means nobody has decided, and should be flagged. The subtraction is the term only this role has: 'nothing comes off' is acceptable only with a reason, and the learner was told to check the widest-reach unowned capability in their register first. Penalize a funding line that pays for a capability by cancelling the control that would detect it going wrong.

dimensions.name: The reckoning is honest about direction, not just about count
dimensions.criteria: All seven claims collected with what was committed and what was concluded. Then the three questions, and the third is the most important thing in the submission: which direction does their judgement lean — systematically assuming better shape than the evidence showed, or worse? Grade whether they answered with a direction AND evidence from their own records, not whether the answer flatters them. Over-estimating organizational readiness is the common pattern; naming it plainly is a top-scoring answer. Credit identifying which single claim moved them most with the specific thing that moved it — a number looked up, a blank they could not fill, a test result they did not expect.

dimensions.name: The delta and the position
dimensions.criteria: Predicted count of true claims against the actual, with an account of the gap — never accuracy. Plus a committed position on the module's claim engaging the real counter-argument: that most things worth doing are irreversible, that irreversible commitment is what makes strategy credible, and that demanding rehearsed rollbacks converts the systems function into a brake. The position must say where the line falls, and the strongest ones notice that the counter-argument is Module 1's reversibility gate turned against the track's own closing artifact — which means a principle is needed rather than a preference.

dimensions.name: One artifact, maintained
dimensions.criteria: The write-up must name exactly ONE artifact from the track — the register, the evaluation plan, the signed decision-rights map, or the exclusion list — that the learner will keep maintaining, plus what would have to be true for it to still be current in a year. A commitment to maintain all four is a commitment to maintain none and should be marked down explicitly. The strongest answers name a trigger or a cadence tied to something that already happens (a quarterly release review, a renewal date, an audit cycle) rather than a resolution to be diligent.
